meta.label: Nappies
meta.attribution: Price is computed from each brand's own listed price and diaper count on the date shown, using the largest comparable pack available, usually Size 4. Materials and certification claims come from each brand's own product or certification pages, checked against the certifying body's own listing where one exists: Bambo Nature's Nordic Swan and EU Ecolabel status is confirmed on Sweden's own ecolabel administrator site, not only the brand's claim. Where a US retailer's own product specification lists 'Industry or Government Certifications: No Certifications,' the note says so; that is not evidence of harm, only the absence of a voluntary third-party label. For context, France's food and environmental safety agency ANSES assessed disposable diapers sold in the French market between 2016 and 2018 without naming individual brands, and found several chemicals, including some fragrances, exceeded ANSES's own safety threshold values in the samples tested. This catalogue cannot say whether that finding applies to any specific product below, only that independent testing of the diaper category as a whole has found real problems, which is part of why a third-party certification like OEKO-TEX or EWG Verified carries more weight than a brand's own marketing claim. US EPA's most recent national estimate put disposable diapers at 4.1 million tons of municipal solid waste in 2018, 1.4 percent of that year's total, with about 3.3 million tons landfilled; every conventional disposable diaper in this list sits inside that same waste stream regardless of brand. UK entries are priced in pence from the retailer's or brand's own page where one lists a price, or from the Which? February 2026 price tracking where the brand only points to retailers; that Which? guide also notes the UK cannot currently recycle disposable nappies, so conventional UK nappies are scored the same way as conventional US ones. EWG Verified claims are checked against EWG's own EWG Verified directory, which listed four diaper brands when checked: ATTITUDE, Coterie, Freestyle and Healthybaby. Reusable cloth nappies are a separate decision in this catalogue. Not medical or safety advice; check the product's own current packaging. Reviewed 2026-08; additions checked 2026-10. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: Pampers Swaddlers

economical.note: Target lists Pampers Swaddlers Sensitive Disposable Diapers, Size 4, 120 count, at $44.99, which is $0.37 per diaper.

environment.note: Target's own product specification for this pack lists 'Industry or Government Certifications: No Certifications.' EPA's national waste inventory separately estimated disposable diapers generated 4.1 million tons of municipal solid waste in 2018, 1.4 percent of that year's total, with about 3.3 million tons landfilled, about four fifths of what was generated; conventional wood-pulp-and-plastic diapers like this one sit inside that stream.

health.note: Target's listing says these diapers are 'Hypoallergenic, and dermatologically approved by the Skin Health Alliance' and 'Free of parabens, elemental chlorine, and latex,' but the same page lists 'No Certifications' under Industry or Government Certifications and notes the diaper contains an added fragrance 'intended to mask odors.'

products.description: The best-known disposable diaper brand, sold at Target and most US grocery and mass retail stores; the retailer's own listing shows no third-party environmental or chemical-safety certification.

products.name: Huggies Little Movers

economical.note: Target lists Huggies Little Movers Disposable Diapers Econ+ Pack, Size 4, 150 count, at $54.99, which is $0.37 per diaper, the same unit price as the equivalent Pampers pack.

environment.note: The same EPA inventory that puts disposable diapers at 4.1 million tons of 2018 municipal solid waste, 1.4 percent of the total, with about 3.3 million tons landfilled, covers this Huggies line too; Target's specification field for this product lists no environmental certification.

health.note: Target's listing states these diapers are 'Paraben-Free, Phthalate-Free, Sulfate-Free, Non-Toxic, No Fragrance Added' and made of wood fluff pulp, but under Industry or Government Certifications the page says 'No Certifications,' and unlike the Pampers and up & up listings in this comparison it makes no hypoallergenic or dermatologist-tested claim.

products.description: Kimberly-Clark's mainstream diaper line, priced the same per diaper as Pampers at this size and carrying the same absence of third-party certification on its Target listing.

products.name: Luvs

economical.note: Target lists Luvs Pro Level Leak Protection Diapers Giant Pack, Size 4, 144 count, at $30.99, which is $0.22 per diaper, about 40 percent less than the equivalent Pampers pack.

environment.note: Luvs sits in the same EPA-tracked disposable diaper waste category as every other conventional diaper in this comparison, 4.1 million tons generated in 2018 and about 3.3 million tons landfilled; Target's specification field for this Luvs pack lists no environmental certification.

health.note: Target's listing describes these diapers as 'Hypoallergenic' and 'No Parabens, No Latex,' with disclosed ingredients petrolatum, stearyl alcohol, and aloe barbadensis leaf extract, but the page lists 'No Certifications' under Industry or Government Certifications, the same as its pricier Pampers sibling from the same manufacturer.

products.description: Procter & Gamble's budget diaper line, cheaper per diaper than its own Pampers brand, with the same materials disclosure and the same lack of third-party certification.

products.name: up & up (Target store brand)

economical.note: Target lists its own up & up Disposable Diapers, Size 4, 200 count, at $36.99, which is $0.18 per diaper, the cheapest of any diaper in this comparison priced by count.

environment.note: This store-brand pack sits in the same EPA-tracked disposable diaper waste category as the national brands, 4.1 million tons of disposable diapers generated in 2018 and about 3.3 million tons landfilled. Target's own certification field for this pack lists 'Meets ASTM Standards, Meets OSHA Requirements' rather than the plain 'No Certifications' shown for Pampers, Huggies, and Luvs, though these are general product standards, not an environmental or chlorine-free ecolabel.

health.note: Target's own product page for its up & up store brand says the diapers are 'Made without elemental chlorine, lotions, latex, fragrances, parabens and phthalates,' 'Hypoallergenic,' and 'Dermatologist Tested,' with a 'comfort-touch liner that is clinically proven to be gentle,' a fuller chemical-exclusion list than Target shows for the national brands it also sells.

products.description: Target's own diaper brand, sold only at Target and target.com; the cheapest option here by unit price, with a longer chemical-exclusion list on its own product page than the national brands carry.

products.name: Millie Moon

economical.note: Target lists Millie Moon Luxury Disposable Diapers, Size 4, 168 count, at $49.99, which is about $0.30 per diaper.

environment.note: Millie Moon is a conventional wood-pulp disposable diaper too, part of the same EPA-tracked waste stream as the mass-market brands: 4.1 million tons of disposable diapers generated in 2018, about 3.3 million tons landfilled. Its Target listing describes the diaper as free of elemental chlorine, but its OEKO-TEX certification, noted below, covers chemical safety testing rather than forest sourcing or an environmental label.

health.note: Target's specification field for this product lists 'Industry or Government Certifications: OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100,' with certificate number HK001 153558 from TESTEX, plus 'Dermatologist tested safe on sensitive skin' and 'quality certified by Dermatest'; the page also states the diapers are vegan and paraben-free with no synthetic fragrance.

products.description: A mid-priced diaper carrying an actual third-party OEKO-TEX certificate number on its Target listing, something the leading national brands in this comparison do not show.

products.name: The Honest Company diapers

environment.note: Honest's own ingredient page says the absorbent core uses elemental-chlorine-free wood pulp from a responsibly managed forest, with 'FSC Certified Fluff Pulp and Other Controlled Material,' and an outer layer of plant-based PLA and polyethylene; this is FSC-certified sourcing but elemental-chlorine-free (ECF) rather than the totally-chlorine-free (TCF) pulp some competitors in this comparison use.

health.note: Honest's product page states the diapers are 'OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 Certified, 3rd party tested for 350 harmful chemicals,' hypoallergenic, fragrance-free, and dermatologist tested, and made without fragrance, elemental chlorine, parabens, or natural rubber latex.

products.description: A widely available branded diaper with FSC-certified pulp and third-party OEKO-TEX testing; price could not be confirmed from an acceptable source and is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: Bambo Nature

environment.note: Sweden's Nordic Swan Ecolabel administrator, which also runs the EU Ecolabel there, returns 58 certified Bambo Nature products in its own product search, including 29 under Diaper and 10 under Diaper (EU-Ecolabel); its listing for Bambo Nature Diapers Size 4 (L) names licensee Abena Produktion A/S and Nordic Swan licence 5023 0001 under the Protective and Absorbent Hygiene Products criteria. Bambo Nature's own certifications page adds FSC-certified pulp sourcing.

health.note: Bambo Nature's own certifications page lists the Asthma Allergy Nordic label, OEKO-TEX Standard 100, Ecocert COSMOS, and 'Dermatologically Tested' alongside its Nordic Swan Ecolabel status, more overlapping third-party marks than most other brands in this comparison disclose in one place.

links.label: Nordic Swan product search: Bambo Nature

products.description: The first diaper brand certified to the Nordic Swan Ecolabel, verifiable on the label administrator's own site rather than only on the brand's word; price could not be confirmed from an acceptable source and is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: Eco by Naty (BioEmbrace)

economical.note: Naty's own site lists a single pack of BioEmbrace Size 1 diapers, 25 count per the page's own product link, at $13.99, which is $0.56 per diaper.

environment.note: Naty's product page describes BioEmbrace as 'the only diaper with certified 100% plant-based materials on skin (verified by DinCertco),' with an FSC-certified cellulose absorbent core and 100 percent recyclable packaging.

health.note: The same page states the diaper is 'verified to strict safety standards against 1,000+ substances incl. chlorine, PFAS, parabens, phthalates (Oeko-Tex Standard 100)' and is 'dermatologically rated Excellent for sensitive skin (Dermatest),' vegan, and free of fragrance, lotion, and latex.

products.description: A plant-based diaper independently verified against a named list of excluded substances, at roughly three times the per-diaper price of the cheapest store brand in this comparison.

products.name: DYPER bamboo diapers

economical.note: Dyper's own monthly box page lists $117.00 for its Newborn size, which the page describes as '204 diapers per delivery (7 changes a day for a month),' which works out to $0.57 per diaper.

environment.note: Dyper's single-pack product page states the diaper is '55% USDA-certified plant-based' with a top and inner cover of viscose from bamboo fibers and a '100% ASTM D6400-certified compostable film,' though the page does not disclose an FSC or Nordic Swan mark the way some competitors do.

health.note: The same page states the diaper carries a '5-star Dermatest rating' and is 'dermatologist-tested for sensitive skin,' without an OEKO-TEX or EWG Verified mark visible on that page.

products.description: A subscription-first bamboo-viscose diaper sold in a monthly box; USDA plant-based content and a compostable film are disclosed on the brand's own page.

products.name: Coterie

economical.note: Coterie's own site lists its subscription at 'Starting at $95/month,' with a Size 4 delivery of 150 diapers; that is $0.63 per diaper, the most expensive in this comparison.

environment.note: Coterie's product page lists totally-chlorine-free (TCF) pulp sourced from sustainably managed forests and states the diaper is made to the EDANA Stewardship Programme Standard, an industry hygiene-sector sustainability framework.

health.note: The same page states the diaper is 'EWG Verified', a mark that restricts parabens, phthalates, heavy metals, pesticides, and VOCs, and says it is 'dermatologist tested + 3rd party lab tested in Germany', made without fragrance, parabens, latex, lotion, chlorine bleaching, or phthalates. EWG's own EWG Verified directory, filtered to diapers, lists eight Coterie diaper sizes, confirming the mark independently.

products.description: A premium subscription diaper with an EWG Verified mark and third-party German lab testing disclosed on its own page, priced far above every other option in this comparison.

products.name: Kudos

economical.note: Kudos's own site lists diapers at $0.45 per diaper one-time, or $0.40 per diaper on its monthly subscription, a 12 percent saving.

environment.note: Kudos's product page describes the absorbent core pulp as 'FSC-certified sustainably harvested wood pulp' that is totally chlorine free, with a cotton topsheet layered over a polyethylene outer film.

health.note: The same page states the diaper is 'OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 certified' and carries the Cotton Natural Seal, made without chlorine, lotion, fragrance, latex, parabens, or phthalates.

products.description: A cotton-topsheet diaper with FSC-certified totally-chlorine-free pulp and OEKO-TEX certification, priced between the store brands and the most expensive subscription diapers here.

products.name: ATTITUDE diapers

environment.note: ATTITUDE's own product page states the absorbent core contains 33 percent wood pulp sourced from 'FSC® eco-managed forests' that is 'Totally Chlorine-Free,' with a bamboo-fiber topsheet and backsheet.

health.note: The same page states the diapers carry 'EWG Verified' certification and 'OEKO-TEX® Standard 100 certification', and are described as completely vegan and free from added fragrance. EWG's own EWG Verified directory, filtered to diapers, lists six ATTITUDE diaper products, confirming the EWG mark independently.

products.description: A bamboo and totally-chlorine-free-pulp diaper carrying both EWG Verified and OEKO-TEX marks on its own product page; a single pack was listed at $16.95 but the diaper count was not shown, so price is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: Diaper bank or community assistance program

economical.note: A nationally representative 2021 survey published in a peer-reviewed journal found 46.1 percent of respondent caregivers reported diaper need (44.0 percent once weighted to national income distribution), and that stores were the most common diaper source at 92.3 percent of acquisitions, while 'an agency or support organization' accounted for only 16.3 percent; the study concludes these community resources are 'unlikely to be adequate given the limited number of families served by diaper banks.'

links.label: National Diaper Bank Network: the need
National Diaper Bank Network: get help now

products.description: A local diaper bank can provide diapers free of charge to families who qualify; the National Diaper Bank Network's own site directs people to call 2-1-1 or search 211.org, or to check its member directory, and notes that SNAP and WIC cannot be used to buy diapers because they are USDA nutrition programs. National survey data shows these programs reach a minority of the families who report going without enough diapers, so this route is free but not reliably available.

products.name: Parent's Choice Dry & Gentle (Walmart store brand)

economical.note: Walmart's own listing for Parent's Choice Dry & Gentle Size 4 shows a 246-count pack at $32.92, 13.4 cents per diaper, and the 192-count pack at $27.97, 14.6 cents per diaper; the largest pack works out to about $0.13 per diaper, the lowest unit price of any US diaper in this comparison. Walmart's page blocks automated readers, so it was read in a full browser.

environment.note: Walmart's listing for this pack names its materials only as super-absorbent polymer, nonwoven, adhesives and elastics, with no pulp-sourcing claim and no environmental certification. Like every conventional disposable here it sits inside the waste stream EPA estimated at 4.1 million tons of disposable diapers generated in 2018, about 3.3 million tons of it landfilled.

health.note: Walmart's listing claims a hypoallergenic liner and lists the diaper as latex-free, with a California Proposition 65 warning field of None; it gives no fragrance, chlorine or paraben exclusion list, no dermatologist testing claim and no third-party chemical certification, a thinner disclosure than Target shows for its own up & up store brand.

products.description: Walmart's own diaper brand and the cheapest per-diaper option in this comparison at the largest pack size; the listing discloses little about materials and no third-party certification.

products.name: Kirkland Signature diapers (Costco)

economical.note: Costco's own page for Kirkland Signature Diaper Sizes 3-7 shows an online price of $39.99, displayed as $0.18 per diaper for the default Size 3 box; its specification lists 198 diapers in the Size 4 box, which at the same listed price is about $0.20 per diaper. Costco sells to members only and the item showed as unavailable for delivery at the address the page defaulted to.

environment.note: Costco's page describes an ultra soft, breathable outer cover but discloses no materials, pulp sourcing or environmental certification. A conventional disposable like this sits inside the waste stream EPA estimated at 4.1 million tons of disposable diapers in 2018, about 3.3 million tons of it landfilled.

health.note: Costco's feature list says the diaper is dermatologically tested for sensitive skin and has a hypoallergenic liner, and its specification marks it hypoallergenic, but the page names no excluded chemicals such as fragrance, chlorine or parabens and shows no third-party chemical certification.

products.description: Costco's own diaper, sold in bulk to members; close to the cheapest per diaper here, with a skin-testing claim but no material disclosure on Costco's page.

products.name: Hello Bello diapers

environment.note: Hello Bello's own product page lists elemental-chlorine-free (ECF) fluff pulp from sustainably managed forests, a plant-derived PLA nonwoven alongside polypropylene, polyethylene and polyester, and says its US factory runs on 100 percent renewable energy and diverts over 80 percent of facility waste from landfill; it names no FSC or ecolabel certificate for any of this. The diaper still ends in the waste stream EPA estimated at 4.1 million tons of disposable diapers in 2018.

health.note: Hello Bello's product page says the diapers are made without phthalates, parabens, lotions, and synthetic fragrances or odor inhibitors, and with ECF rather than totally chlorine-free pulp; the page shows no third-party chemical certification such as OEKO-TEX or EWG Verified, and Hello Bello is not among the brands EWG lists in its own EWG Verified diaper directory.

products.description: A US-made diaper sold by subscription and at Walmart and Amazon, with a plant-derived liner and a stated exclusion list but no third-party certificate; its own site sells boxes of seven packs without stating diapers per pack, so price is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: Rascals Premium Diapers

environment.note: Rascals' own product page describes the absorbent core and hot-air-bonded materials but discloses no pulp sourcing, plant-based content or environmental certification, so it is scored as a conventional disposable inside the waste stream EPA estimated at 4.1 million tons of disposable diapers in 2018, about 3.3 million tons landfilled.

health.note: Rascals' product page states '0% Lotions, Latex or Fragrance' and, under its certifications heading, 'Hypoallergenic & dermatologist tested safe on skin', but lists no third-party chemical certificate such as OEKO-TEX; the page sends US buyers to Walmart rather than giving a pack count and price, so price is left out.

products.description: An Australian-founded diaper sold in the US mainly through Walmart, with a fragrance, lotion and latex exclusion and dermatologist testing but no third-party chemical certificate on its own page.

products.name: Healthybaby Our Diaper

economical.note: Healthybaby's own page prices a box of 6 packs at $105, one-time or by subscription, and states Size 4 packs hold 25 diapers, so a Size 4 box is 150 diapers at about $0.70 each, more than any other priced diaper in this comparison except ECO BOOM.

environment.note: Healthybaby's product page says the absorbent core is sustainably harvested wood pulp that is 'TCF (Totally Chlorine Free) and 100% FSC certified' and that 'the outer cover contains 15% organic cotton', the same totally-chlorine-free FSC pulp profile as the higher-rated diapers in this comparison, though like all of them it still relies on plastic super-absorbent polymer.

health.note: EWG's own EWG Verified product directory, filtered to diapers, lists Healthybaby among only four diaper brands carrying the mark (with ATTITUDE, Coterie and Freestyle), confirming the claim on Healthybaby's page that its diaper is EWG Verified; the brand's page adds a Microbiome-Friendly certification, dermatologist testing, and exclusion of parabens, phthalates, fragrance, latex, lotion and PFAS.

products.description: A premium subscription diaper whose EWG Verified mark checks out in EWG's own directory, with totally-chlorine-free FSC pulp, at roughly five times the per-diaper price of the cheapest store brand.

products.name: ECO BOOM bamboo diapers

economical.note: ECO BOOM's own subscription page lists Size 4 (L, 9-14 kg) at 120 diapers per delivery, priced at $87.98 in the store's own product data, about $0.73 per diaper, the most expensive priced diaper in this comparison; its trial pack is the same unit price, 60 diapers for $43.99.

environment.note: ECO BOOM's page lists a topsheet and backsheet of 100 percent viscose from bamboo, a 'Chlorine-Free Wood Pulp + SAP' core, a breathable film of 'PE + Calcium Carbonate', FSC-certified pulp and 30 percent recycled-plastic inner bags, and claims 30 percent less plastic than a standard diaper; unlike DYPER it does not claim a certified-compostable film, and the FSC claim names no certificate number.

health.note: Dermatest's own reference database records an ECO BOOM bamboo diaper patch test 'on 30 subjects with sensetive skin' in which 'No subject showed any irritative skin reactions', and confirms the product received its Dermatest Guarantee Seal; ECO BOOM's own page adds that the diapers contain no dye or chlorine, but this is a skin-irritation test, not a chemical-content certificate.

products.description: A bamboo-viscose subscription diaper shipped within the contiguous US, with an independently listed skin test and the highest per-diaper price in this comparison.

products.name: Aldi Mamia nappies

economical.note: Aldi's own UK product page lists Mamia Nappies Size 4 Jumbo, 84 nappies, at £4.89, which Aldi shows as £0.06 per nappy, the lowest unit price in this comparison; The February 2026 Which? guide separately found Aldi, Tesco, Lidl, Ocado and Sainsbury's own-brand size 4 nappies all averaging about 6.1p each over its July 2023 to June 2024 price tracking.

environment.note: The February 2026 Which? disposable nappy guide says the UK does not currently have the facilities to process disposable nappies properly and lists being unrecyclable in the UK among their drawbacks; Aldi's own product page names no materials, pulp sourcing or ecolabel for Mamia, so it is scored as a conventional disposable.

products.description: Aldi's own nappy and the cheapest per nappy in this comparison; Aldi's page states features and price but nothing about materials or chemical exclusions, so no chemical-safety score is given.

products.name: Kit & Kin eco nappies

economical.note: Kit & Kin's own page sells a 38-nappy pack of Size 4 at £8.99 one-time, about 24p per nappy, and a four-pack subscription with 20 percent off and free delivery; that is roughly four times Aldi's Mamia per nappy.

environment.note: B Lab's own directory lists Kit and Kin Ltd as a Certified B Corporation since August 2022 with a current overall B Impact score of 87.8, against 80 to qualify; that is a company-level certification, not a product ecolabel. The product page lists sugar-cane-derived outer and inner linings, totally chlorine free fluff pulp and paper packaging, and says the nappies are made in a carbon neutral EU plant, but names no FSC or Nordic Swan certificate.

health.note: Kit & Kin's product page says its products are 'made without chlorine processing, latex, lotions, fragrances, most common allergens, phthalates, optical brighteners, or organotins' and describes the nappies as hypoallergenic and dermatologist approved; it shows no OEKO-TEX or EWG certificate number.

products.description: A UK subscription nappy from a certified B Corp, with plant-based linings, totally-chlorine-free pulp and a long chemical-exclusion list, at about four times the per-nappy price of supermarket own brands.

products.name: Pampers Baby-Dry (UK)

economical.note: The February 2026 Which? guide tracked a 44-pack of Pampers Baby-Dry size 4 from July 2023 to June 2024 and found average prices from 18p a nappy at Asda to 27p at Boots, against about 6.1p for supermarket own-brand size 4 nappies over the same period; its own figures predate this check, and Pampers' site sends buyers to retailers rather than listing a price.

environment.note: The Which? guide notes that the UK does not currently have facilities to process disposable nappies properly; Pampers' own Baby-Dry page lists no FSC, Nordic Swan or other environmental certification for this line, unlike its Harmonie range, so it is scored as a conventional disposable.

health.note: Pampers' own UK Baby-Dry page says the nappy is 'Tested and certified according to Standard 100 by OEKO-TEX' and 'Dermatologically tested and made without EU perfume allergens' regulated under the EU Cosmetics Regulation, and carries Skin Health Alliance approval; the page does not give an OEKO-TEX certificate number, so the claim rests on the brand's statement.

products.description: The best-known UK nappy, priced three to four times supermarket own brands per nappy in the Which? tracking, with an OEKO-TEX claim on its own UK page that the US Pampers listing in this comparison does not show.

products.name: Pampers Harmonie (UK)

environment.note: The February 2026 Which? guide notes that the UK does not currently have facilities to process disposable nappies properly; Pampers' own Harmonie page displays an FSC mark among its certifications, the only Pampers UK line checked here to do so, but names no certificate number or how much of the pulp it covers.

health.note: Pampers' UK Harmonie page lists '0% perfume and lotion', says the nappy is 'Hypoallergenic* and dermatologically tested', and displays OEKO-TEX Standard 100, British Skin Foundation and DermaTest marks; no certificate number is given, so these rest on the brand's own page. Price is left out because the page sends buyers to retailers.

products.description: Pampers' gentler UK line, free of perfume and lotion and showing FSC and OEKO-TEX marks on its own page; the closest UK equivalent to the Pampers Pure line, which no longer appears in Pampers' US product range.
